source.title: The Geometry of Harmful Intent: Training-Free Anomaly Detection via Angular Deviation in LLM Residual Streams

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether harmful-intent information remains detectable after refusal-direction ablation, using an angular anomaly detector rather than directly testing refusal behavior.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-prompt detection in abliterated models and compares it with instruction-tuned counterparts. It does not test the original difference-in-means direction by ablating it at every layer and position, adding it, or measuring refusal rates. Its K=1 results concern a normative-reference detector, not whether refusal itself is mediated by one direction.
record.test_reason: The study removes the refusal direction by weight orthogonalisation (abliterated checkpoints) and tests whether harmful-prompt information stays readable in the residual stream. That bears on V5, whether harmfulness is encoded separately from the refusal mechanism. It uses a different method: an external angular detector, not the model's own judgment. It does not measure refusal rates, ablate or add the difference-in-means direction itself, or test capability retention, so V1 and V2 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that harm recognition and refusal generation are separable: abliteration leaves harmful-intent geometry intact in both Qwen families. They say base-model parity suggests this geometry forms in pretraining. They call for non-Qwen and JailbreakBench validation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a PC1 fitted only to safe prompts and angular anomaly scores to detect harmful prompts; it does not use the original harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction to intervene on refusal behavior. It evaluates checkpoints described as abliterated rather than directly testing refusal rates.
record.method_sensitivity: Operating layer varies: layer 20 for all models except Qwen2.5-0.5B-Abliterated, reported at layer 10. The paper reports opposite harmful-versus-normative angular orientations across the two model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Base (pretrained) models detect harmful prompts as well as or slightly better than instruct models (AUROC h/n 0.9642 vs 0.9497; 0.9585 vs 0.9420).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The harmful-prompt representation exploited by the detector exists before alignment fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: A single PC1 fitted on safe prompts beats K>1 detectors by 0.033–0.063 AUROC in all six models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful-vs-normative separation is near one-dimensional relative to the normative principal direction. This is not the refusal direction.

record.problems: The evaluation is limited to two Qwen model families from one vendor and uses AdvBench; the authors note harmful-prompt compactness may reflect shared prompt syntax and call for evaluation on structurally diverse data. The operating layer is selected by maximising AUROC on the harmful evaluation set, and the authors identify this as a source of selection bias. No direct refusal-behavior or general-capability evaluation is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results omitted. K-ablation and other detector-baseline comparisons were not included because they do not test whether refusal itself is mediated by one direction or whether harmfulness judgment is a model behavior separate from refusal.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is ablated or added, and no refusal rates or capability checks are reported.
Abliterated checkpoints are used, but whether they stop refusing, or keep other abilities, is not evaluated.
Jailbreaks and adversarial training are untested. Adversarial prompts against the detector are explicitly left open.
The K=1 vs K>1 comparison concerns a PC1 fitted on safe prompts for detection, not the dimensionality of refusal.
The model's own harmfulness judgment, a causal separation, and models beyond two small Qwen families are untested. The harmful set is only AdvBench, which may reflect shared syntax.
No transfer of the refusal direction is tested.
Base and instruct models are compared only for harm detection, not for whether a removable refusal direction exists.

missing.what: Angular statistics showing the two-ring geometry is unchanged after abliteration (e.g. Δθ +0.623 Chat vs +0.627 Abliterated; σharm 0.030 vs 0.031). This is further V5 evidence.
Harmful-vs-rest (h/r) AUROC for the abliterated models (0.9674, 0.9577) and their instruct counterparts (0.9661, 0.9609).

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Abliterated models are third-party Hugging Face checkpoints, and the study never measures their refusal behaviour. The operating layer is selected on the harmful evaluation set, which the authors acknowledge as selection bias. The text contains no instructions.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is ablated or added, and refusal behavior or preservation of general capabilities is not evaluated.
The study uses abliterated checkpoints and describes them as unable to refuse, but does not report a refusal-behavior evaluation of the weight edit.
No jailbreak suppression of the direction or training against its ablation is tested.
The K=1 versus K>1 detector comparison does not test whether refusal is represented by an affine structure, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
The study tests detection of harmful prompts from activations after refusal-direction ablation, not a model-generated harmfulness judgment or the separate decision circuit directly.
No transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct checkpoints is tested.
Base, instruction-tuned, and abliterated variants are compared for detection, but the study does not test how or when refusal training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.

relationships.condition: Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen2.5-0.5B abliterated checkpoints, AdvBench harmful vs Alpaca/XSTest prompts, external angular detector
relationships.reason: After abliteration, harmful-vs-normative AUROC stays within 0.002–0.005 of the instruct models (R1, R2), and harmful-vs-benign-aggressive AUROC stays 1.000 (R3, R4). Harm information persists without the refusal direction. Caveats: refusal removal is not verified, and the AdvBench template may drive the signal.
relationships.display_finding: Harmful-versus-normative AUROC stayed within 0.002–0.005 of instruct models, and harmful-versus-benign-aggressive AUROC remained 1.000, although refusal removal was unverified and prompt templates could drive discrimination.

labels.reason: After abliteration, AUROC h/n is 0.9517 vs 0.9497 and 0.9374 vs 0.9420, and h/b stays 1.000 (R1-R4). The evidence is correlational. Refusal removal is not verified, and the template caveat is untested, so it is not a limits_scope result.

relation.reason: It compares base, instruct and abliterated variants and draws an explicit dissociation conclusion (harm recognition is separable from refusal). This goes beyond reporting only detector performance.

tranche.reason: The study uses a different method (an angular anomaly detector fitted on safe-prompt PC1) on abliterated vs instruct checkpoints. It reports its own result that harm geometry survives refusal-direction removal, which bears on V5.

source_check.notes: Both abliterated checkpoints are third-party (prithivMLmods Gliese-...-Abliterated-Caption, huihui-ai), so the test_reason line "the study removes" is inaccurate. The paper is internally inconsistent: the abstract and contributions say the abliterated models score "at most 0.015 below" instruct, but Sections 5.2-5.3 give +0.002 and -0.005 (0.015 is the base-instruct gap). The operating layer was chosen by argmax on the harmful eval set.

statements.problem: The numbers and layers for this study are correct. 'No controls' is defensible because there is no intervention control. The XSTest benign-aggressive set is only a wording contrast.

statements.correction: The authors call the AdvBench template 'the most parsimonious explanation' of sigma_theta_harm of 0.030-0.052 rad (Section 8). This is untested; JailbreakBench evaluation is proposed as future work. h/b AUROC is 1.000 against 250 XSTest benign-aggressive prompts in all six variants. Under the rules, an untested part should not be a limits_scope citation.
statements.problem: The facts are right (h/b AUROC is 1.000 in all six variants, including Base), but the study shows no result that the signal is wording-level. The AdvBench-template explanation is the authors' untested hypothesis about harmful-cluster compactness (sigma_theta), not about AUROC. h/b = 1.000 separates AdvBench harmful prompts from XSTest aggressive-but-benign wording. The study's own verdict is only V5 supports, with no limits_scope.

Correct for this study: the model's own harm judgment and any refusal behaviour are not measured. The authors say abliteration renders the models unable to refuse but don't test it. The measure is an unsupervised angular anomaly score, not a trained probe. The count weight_edit.studies = 1 looks low, since this study's R1-R4 are weight_edit rows, but it can't be checked from this text.
h/b AUROC 1.000 in every variant, including Base, is correct (Table 1, Section 5.2).

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Abliterated AUROC h/n is 0.9374 at L10. The L20 value differs by <0.004 (Section 4.7, Table 1 †). Per-layer AUROC varies by <0.08 across all 24 layers in every model. The baseline is Instruct 0.9420 at L20.
statements.problem: The layer mismatch is stated correctly. Listing it as a layer sensitivity leaves out that the paper reports almost no layer dependence for this comparison.

statements.correction: Compactness is sigma_theta_harm 0.030-0.052 rad vs sigma_theta_norm 0.183-0.272 rad (Table 2, Section 6.3). The authors propose the AdvBench template as an explanation and name JailbreakBench as the key open experiment. h/b AUROC 1.000 is a separate result (Table 1).
statements.problem: The template effect is an untested hypothesis by the authors, not a measured sensitivity: the study never varies the prompt template. 'Compactness' is the sigma_theta measure, not the AUROC 1.000 ceiling the parenthetical gives.
The shown text makes no claim specific to this study. Its correlational, supports-only V5 verdict fits the counts and the 'mostly correlational' framing.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The two tested abliterated Qwen variants, using the reported normative-reference angular detector
reader_labels.reason: Harmful-prompt detection remains close to the instruction-tuned reference for h/n and is perfect for h/b after refusal-direction ablation, supporting a distinction between detectable harmful-intent geometry and the removed refusal mechanism; this does not directly test a model-generated harmfulness judgment (R1–R4).
